extent to which this moisture accumulates depends on the effectiveness of ventilation and 
extraction systems (see Section 4.3). 
While RH decreases as air warms, the main risk to buildings occurs when RH increases as

environment. Under these conditions, the relative humidity of the air adjacent to the 
surface can approach saturation and lead to condensation.

4.5 Saturation and dew point 
Temperature determines the maximum amount of water molecules that air can hold. When 
this limit is reached, the air is saturated. If the air cools beyond this point, the excess water 
vapour condenses into mist or liquid droplets until a new saturation limit is reached at the 
lower temperature. 
The relationship between temperature and water vapour can be visualised using a 
psychrometric chart. 9 Figure 4.5 shows a simplified chart used for introductory purposes. 
A key feature of the chart is the diagonal curve that separates the gridded vapour zone

intersects this curve represents the saturation limit for that temperature. Reading 
horizontally from this point to the vertical axis indicates the water vapour content of the air 
at saturation. This curve (also called the dew point line ) represents the dew point 
condition for each temperature.

What is dew point? 
Dew point is the temperature at which the RH of the air reaches 100% saturation, and 
water vapour contained in the air begins to condense. A higher dew point indicates that 
the air contains more water vapour. Conversely, a lower dew point indicates drier air. 
Relative humidity alone does not indicate how much water vapour is present unless 
temperature and pressure are also known.

4.6 Relative humidity, comfort, health and mould risk 
Relative humidity plays a critical role in indoor comfort and health. When RH is too low, the 
air becomes excessively dry, causing irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory 
membranes, and contributing to dehydration and fatigue. These symptoms are common in 
environments such as passenger aircraft cabins, where RH is often around 10%. For 
comfort, RH of 30%– 60% is commonly suggested, although this range does not relate to 
any specific temperature.

High RH can interfere with the body’s natural cooling mechanism by reducing the 
evaporation of sweat, leading to discomfort and a “sticky” sensation. Elevated RH can also 
increase the likelihood of mould and fungal growth. Within the 30%–60% RH range, house 
dust mites (which release allergens) also thrive.

health risks. At lower temperatures, such as when heating is reduced or switched off 
overnight, RH can rise further and may approach levels associated with an increased risk 
of mould growth.

air reaches its dew point and condensation becomes visible.

4.7 Material responses to relative humidity 
The response of different building materials to RH is a key consideration in condensation 
management. Many common building materials are hygroscopic, meaning they can absorb 
or adsorb moisture from their surroundings. This behaviour influences how moisture 
moves through the building fabric and affects both the extent and consequences of any 
condensation that forms. 
Hygroscopic materials attract and retain water vapour from surrounding air. Adsorption 
typically occurs first and involves the attachment of water vapour molecules to the 
microscopic surfaces of porous materials without forming liquid water. This interaction 
can significantly influence material performance and durability. 
As hygroscopic materials approach their adsorption capacity, they can also take in liquid 
water through capillary suction (wicking) and absorption, storing moisture within pores 
and cracks. For example, timber can increase its moisture content to around 25–30% at 
about 98% RH by adsorbing water vapour from the air. Timber that becomes saturated by 
liquid water can hold several times more moisture in its pore structure. A material’s ability 
to adsorb and store moisture depends not only on its material properties, but also on the 
vapour pressure and temperature of the surrounding air. 
Hygroscopic materials respond primarily to RH, rather than the absolute amount of water 
vapour in air. They absorb more moisture when RH is high and release it as RH falls. 
Because RH increases as air temperatures fall, cooler conditions tend to promote greater 
water vapour storage within hygroscopic materials. This behaviour can provide a 
temporary hygric buffer, moderating changes in moisture levels as water vapour levels 
increase or temperatures fall. 
However, experience shows that relying on the hygric capacity of the building envelope 
alone is not a reliable strategy for preventing moisture problems. Some of this capacity is 
needed to manage periodic wetting from rain, surface water or rising groundwater. 
Construction moisture within the building fabric itself (such as water retained in concrete 
slabs or in steam-cured concrete blocks) must also be considered.

When unwanted water appears inside a building, it is often mistaken for a plumbing or

accumulate, run, drip and pond, sometimes causing damage well away from where 
condensation first occurred. These situations are known as phantom or ghost leaks. A 
strong indicator of a phantom leak is the appearance of water in the absence of recent 
rainfall or plumbing use. 
4.8 Water vapour diffusion through materials 
While most water vapour in buildings is transported by moving air, some also moves by 
diffusion. Water vapour molecules can pass through materials that block liquid water and 
even air. When there is a higher concentration of water vapour on one side of a material 
than on the other, vapour will naturally diffuse through the material towards the lower 
concentration.

materials that are permeable to water vapour. Each bar represents a typical range for the 
material. Materials that are effectively impermeable to water vapour, such as glass and 
most metals, prevent diffusion and therefore would not appear on the chart.

4.9 Climate 
When considering condensation, at least two climates need to be taken into account: 
• the outdoor climate , shaped by local weather conditions, and 
• the indoor climate , which may be intentionally controlled through design or may arise 
incidentally from building use. 
Indoor conditions are influenced by occupants’ activities and by how they respond to 
changing outdoor conditions to maintain comfort. The outdoor and indoor environments 
are inherently connected, as buildings must bring in fresh outdoor air and expel stale 
indoor air through ventilation, infiltration and exfiltration. 
The exchange of heat, air and water vapour across the building enclosure – through 
surfaces that appear solid – determines the temperature and moisture conditions within 
interstitial spaces of the building envelope (see Figure 4.9). These interstitial conditions 
play a critical role in condensation risk.

4.9.1 Climate classifications 
Climate classification systems used in building design typically focus on environmental 
factors that affect human comfort. Using this approach, relatively broad groupings can be 
sufficient to set fundamental thermal design strategies. For example, as few as four basic 
climate types are commonly used for this purpose (Szokolay 1995). 
The four basic climate types are as follows. 
• Cold climates : Conditions in which people feel too cold outdoors for most or all of 
the year, due to low temperatures or excessive heat loss. 
• Temperate climates: Conditions characterised by insufficient heat in the coolest 
season and excess heat in the warmest season, although neither is particularly 
severe. 
• Hot dry climates: Conditions with high outdoor temperatures and relatively low 
humidity, allowing effective evaporative cooling of the body. Day–night temperature 
variations are typically large, with cooler nights providing relief from daytime heat. 
• Warm humid climates: Conditions with high temperatures and high humidity, where 
limited evaporation reduces cooling effectiveness. Small diurnal (day-night) 
temperature variations mean warm conditions persist overnight. 
The eight climate zones used by the NCC energy efficiency provisions are subdivisions of 
these four basic climate types. They reflect differences in typical temperatures and the

4.10 Outdoor condensation potential 
In the absence of a single accepted method for assessing condensation risk across all 
climates, Australian building practitioners can draw on local climate information. Among 
the most useful sources are the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) climate statistics, which 
provide monthly mean minimum and maximum temperatures averaged over the period of 
record for each weather station. These records also include monthly mean dew point 
temperatures for 9am and 3pm, which indicate the atmospheric water vapour content at 
those times. 
Figure 4.10 compares the average dew point (shown as a dotted blue curve) with the 
monthly mean minimum temperature (shown as a red/purple curve). Where the mean 
minimum temperature falls below the dew point temperature, condensation may occur 
under suitable surface and exposure conditions. As illustrated by the blue shaded area in 
Figure 4.10, this potential is not limited to the colder months. In some locations, the 
combinations of temperature and water vapour required for condensation can occur in any 
season. 
The yellow curve in Figure 4.10 represents the monthly mean maximum temperature and 
provides context for likely daytime conditions following overnight condensation events. In 
many Australian locations, nights that allow condensation to form are typically followed by 
warmer daytime conditions that promote drying. As a result, condensation may be 
temporary and have limited long-term impact.

4.11 Indoor climate and water vapour loads 
Differences in temperature and water vapour content between outdoor and indoor 
environments strongly influence building envelope design and detailing. Because air is 
continually exchanged between indoors and outdoors, indoor water vapour levels 
generally reflect outdoor conditions unless moisture is actively reduced through effective 
dehumidification. While this may occur in some air-conditioned buildings, depending on 
plant capacity and control settings, it is uncommon in Australian homes, particularly during 
the heating season. 
For design purposes during the heating season, it is therefore conservative to assume that 
outdoor water vapour content represents the starting point for indoor humidity conditions. 
Daily average indoor water vapour levels in homes generally depend on several interacting 
factors, including: 
• the amount of outdoor air introduced through ventilation 
• internal sources of water vapour 
• the amount of water vapour that can be vented directly outdoors 
• the rate at which water vapour is removed through ongoing ventilation.

Effective moisture management requires an understanding of both outdoor and indoor 
climate conditions. 
Assessment typically involves: 
• assessing the local outdoor climate using psychrometric charts and BoM climate 
data to understand temperature and humidity patterns, comfort zones, and 
seasonal variation 
• estimating likely indoor conditions by considering ventilation rates, internal moisture

5 Creating dry buildings 
5.1 Overview 
This chapter outlines practical strategies for minimising condensation and supporting the 
delivery of dry buildings. It focuses on how building design and construction decisions 
influence moisture behaviour and condensation outcomes. 
The chapter addresses: 
• the design and performance of building envelopes 
• indoor environmental conditions, including relative humidity 
• condensation within interstitial spaces 
• the role of control layers for water, air, vapour and thermal control 
• approaches to assessing condensation risk, including calculation methods and 
relevant software tools. 
Together, these topics are intended to support practitioners in applying the concepts 
outlined in earlier chapters and in understanding how different design and construction 
choices can influence condensation performance. Unless otherwise stated, the strategies 
discussed are explanatory and should be read in conjunction with the relevant NCC 
provisions.

5.2 Envelopes (claddings, linings and control layers) 
Once a building is enclosed and occupied, its internal environment will differ from the 
external environment. These differences are usually most noticeable during the hottest 
and coldest weather, when heating or cooling is used. 
Differences in temperature, air pressure, and water vapour conditions (including dew 
point) across the building envelope drive the movement of heat, air and moisture. The 
building envelope must manage these flows to limit condensation risk and support indoor 
comfort and durability.

Effective condensation management relies on appropriate design and construction of the 
building envelope, combined with strategies to control internal moisture sources. 
Adequate ventilation is essential to limit moisture accumulation and reduce the likelihood 
of condensation. 
To manage RH and condensation, four interrelated layers of control are typically involved: 
• Water control : The first priority is to control liquid water. Rain and groundwater are 
the main causes of surface wetting, and, if poorly managed, can penetrate deeper 
into the building fabric. Wet building elements are more vulnerable to condensation 
and are slower to dry. 
• Air control : Because water vapour and heat are transported with air, the envelope 
should guide air movement along intentional pathways as much as possible. 
Uncontrolled leakage through gaps, cracks and penetrations can undermine efforts to 
manage moisture and heat flow. 
• Water vapour control : Water vapour can also move through permeable materials by 
diffusion. Vapour control does not require completely blocking this movement. In 
many cases, slowing diffusion during one season while allowing drying during 
another can be beneficial. Appropriate strategies depend on climate, building use and 
envelope construction, and must remain consistent with NCC requirements. 
• Heat control : The NCC sets minimum energy efficiency requirements in Section J of 
Volume One and Section H of Volume Two. These provisions specify minimum 
thermal resistance (R-Value) requirements for walls, floors and roofs by climate zone. 
Meeting these requirements helps to control heat flow, support internal surface 
temperatures remaining above the dew point, and support indoor conditions with 
acceptable RH. Where the NCC specifies vapour permeance requirements, meeting 
these requirements supports drying of interstitial spaces, particularly in cold climates. 
In hot, humid climates, air-conditioning can create cooled surfaces that promote 
condensation, highlighting the need for appropriate vapour control strategies. 
Ideally, a single material would provide all four control functions across the entire building 
envelope. In practice, factors such as weather exposure, durability requirements, cost, 
and construction methods mean that multiple materials are usually required. These 
materials together form the control layers within the interstitial spaces between exterior 
claddings and interior linings (see Figure 5.1).

5.3 Changes to interstitial conditions in the building 
envelope 
Changes in environmental conditions, regulatory requirements and construction practices 
have altered the moisture and temperature conditions within buildings. In combination, 
these changes can increase the likelihood of condensation within the interstitial spaces of 
the building envelope. 
Interstitial condensation risk is commonly associated with higher indoor RH and cooler 
surface temperatures that approach the dew point of indoor air. These conditions may 
arise because of increased airtightness, higher levels of insulation, changes in material 
selection, and evolving patterns of building use. 
Effective management of interstitial condensation relies on proportionate design and 
construction measures that both limit moisture ingress and support adequate moisture 
removal and drying within the building envelope.

5.5 Condensation in interstitial spaces 
Figure 5.2 illustrates typical locations within the building envelope where condensation 
may form during the heating season. Identifying these locations is a useful starting point. 
However, the presence of condensation alone does not determine risk. The key 
considerations are: 
• the quantity of condensate that forms 
• the length of time it remains in liquid form before drying can occur 
• the potential for moisture to wick, flow , or drip from the condensing surface 
• which other building elements may be affected as a result. 
The location of the insulation layer – whether internal, within a cavity or external – has a 
strong influence on where damaging condensation is most likely to occur. A useful starting 
question when assessing roofs, walls or floors is: 
‘Where is the coldest surface in this wall, floor, or roof where condensation could lead 
to damage?’ 
Figure 5.4 illustrates this approach by identifying critical condensation surfaces within a 
masonry veneer wall. 
In NCC Climate zone 1, which is characterised by very humid summers and warm winters, 
the layer immediately behind the interior lining is often the coldest surface at risk of 
condensation when spaces are mechanically cooled. This risk increases when

5.6.1 Roof cladding condensate 
Condensation beneath roof cladding commonly occurs when moist air in the roof space 
comes into contact with the underside of the roof covering. This risk is particularly 
evident under metal roofing, where night-sky radiative cooling can cause the roof surface 
temperature to fall several degrees below the surrounding air temperature. 
To manage the risk of condensation in roof spaces, the NCC includes requirements for 
roof-space ventilation in Clauses F8D5 and F8D6 of Volume One and Clauses 10.8.3 and 
10.8.4 of the Housing Provisions. These provisions also apply to tiled roofs that

In addition to ventilation, condensation risk beneath metal roofing can further be reduced 
by installing a roof blanket or sarking. Sarking can intercept condensate forming on the 
underside of the roof sheeting and direct it toward gutters. In this role, the sarking 
functions as a water control layer, or drainage plane, preventing moisture from dripping 
onto ceiling linings or insulation below. 
While sarking must be waterproof, it does not necessarily need to have a high resistance 
to water vapour. In some situations, the ability of sarking to absorb and temporarily hold 
water can be beneficial – particularly where condensate levels are high and drainage paths 
to gutters are limited. This may occur under low-pitched roofs, where the roof sheet 
profiles or fixings restrict water flow. 
Where sarking is impermeable to water vapour, condensation forming above it is largely 
driven by humid outdoor air circulating through the roof covering and cavities. Figure 5.5 
illustrates how condensation can form on the underside of roof cladding when night-sky 
cooling causes the cladding temperature to fall below the dew point of the external air 
moving through roof corrugations. In these situations, effective drainage is essential to 
avoid moisture accumulation. 
Condensation may also form on the underside of the sarking itself. This risk can be 
reduced by ventilating the roof space to lower humidity levels. Installing sarking below 
battens, rather than directly beneath the roof cladding, can further reduce this risk by 
limiting heat transfer from the roof covering. 
The use of spacers or battens can interrupt thermal bridging between the roof cladding 
and the sarking, raising the sarking temperature and reducing the likelihood of 
condensation. These spacers can also improve drainage and ventilation above the sarking. 
This approach is illustrated in industry guidance such as the Australian Steel Institute’s 
(ASI) Condensation Management for Steel Roofing. The ASI illustration also shows gaps at 
the top of the sarking under the ridge capping to allow ventilation to be maintained under 
the sarking.

Comparing the monthly average outdoor dew point with the mean minimum temperature 
provides useful insight into the relative risk of roof-cladding condensation (see 
Section 4.10). Analysis of climate data for approximately 160 Australian locations shows 
that roof-cladding condensation is likely to occur in 95 locations, even without accounting 
for night-sky cooling. Reducing mean minimum temperatures by as little as 2°C to reflect 
radiative cooling increases this number to around 140 locations, indicating that most roofs 
are at risk of at least occasional condensation. Climate data can also be used to evaluate 
daytime drying potential and the role of roof-space ventilation in reducing the risk of 
persistent moisture. 
Clay and concrete roof tiles provide some thermal mass and can absorb limited moisture 
on their undersides, reducing the likelihood of dripping condensation. However, a 
waterproof sarking may still be required to manage water ingress through tile joints or 
wind-driven rain. In these situations, a highly vapour-permeable sarking can provide 
waterproofing while allowing water vapour to escape, taking advantage of ventilation 
through the tiled roof covering to help lower the dew point in the roof space.

influences the ability of building elements in contact with the ground to store and dry 
moisture. For this reason careful detailing of the water control layer is essential at 
interfaces where the building envelope meets the ground (see Figure 5.6).

To reduce water and vapour pressure beneath slabs and to provide a capillary break, a 
100 mm granular drainage bed is commonly used. This bed is typically formed from coarse 
aggregate and is intended to: 
• drain liquid water away from the building base, and 
• support drying of the sub-slab environment, depending on site conditions. 
A single pliable membrane with high resistance to both liquid water and water vapour 
transmission may be used to combine the water and water vapour control functions 
beneath the slab. This membrane is often detailed to turn up along the external face of the 
slab and is commonly positioned inside rigid insulation. The insulation is typically 
protected by a water-tolerant facing material, such as fibre-cement sheet, which may be 
primed on both faces and all edges to resist moisture exposure. 
In practice, insulation and its protective facing may be installed in the formwork before the 
slab is poured. Materials selected for this location should be resistant to moisture 
exposure and rigid enough to withstand handling, impact and backfilling pressures. 
Together, these measures support compliance with NCC provisions that require buildings 
in contact with the ground to manage the ingress of moisture and water vapour, while 
allowing drying of the building fabric where appropriate.

However, where air leakage follows longer or more convoluted paths through cooler parts 
of the building fabric, water vapour may cool to its dew point and condense. Such leakage 
paths have been estimated to account for approximately 5–10% of total moist air flow

some condensation risk assessment methods. However, where air leakage is reasonably 
well controlled, vapour diffusion through materials can become the dominant mechanism 
influencing interstitial moisture accumulation and condensation risk.

Where the dew point temperature of the air is substantially higher than the temperature of 
interstitial surfaces, limiting water vapour movement towards colder surfaces can reduce 
the risk of condensation under certain conditions. 
However, Australian research and overseas experience show that this approach does not 
perform well in all climates or seasons. A vapour control layer that reduces condensation

In very cold climates, vapour barriers have traditionally been located on the warm side of 
the building envelope to limit the migration of warm, moisture-laden indoor air into 
progressively colder outer layers. 
In hot, humid tropical climates, a similar approach has been applied by locating vapour 
barriers on the external side of the envelope to limit water vapour movement towards 
cooled interior surfaces in air-conditioned buildings. 
These approaches can work in climates that are consistently cold, or consistently warm 
and humid. In climates with mixed seasonal conditions, however, experience shows that 
vapour barriers often create more problems than they resolve. 
While some locations in Australia experience a predominantly single season climate, most 
are characterised by seasonal variability. Increasing use of air-conditioning further 
complicates vapour flow behaviour by reversing the direction of vapour drive during 
summer, making it difficult to identify a single suitable location for a vapour barrier. 
Building-science research, including work by John Straube (2001) and observations by 
Lstiburek (2011), consistently indicates that: 
In many practical situations, a low-permeance vapour barrier will not improve 
hygrothermal performance and may in fact increase the likelihood of damaging 
condensation or trapping moisture in the system. A common misconception regarding 
low-permeance vapour barriers is that their inclusion where one is not technically 
needed provides an extra level of performance and resistance to moisture problems. 
Quite the opposite is true. 
Lstiburek’s work on moisture management emphasises balancing the need to limit 
moisture ingress with the need to allow assemblies to dry. Key principles, paraphrased 
below (Lstiburek 2011b), include: 
• preferring vapour retarders over vapour barriers where lower resistance is sufficient 
• avoiding vapour retarders where vapour-permeable materials can achieve the 
required performance 
• avoiding vapour barriers on both sides of an assembly, so drying can occur in at least 
one direction 
• recognising that vapour barriers on interior surfaces can increase condensation risk

5.8.2 Water vapour control under floors 
The suspended timber-framed floor illustrated in Figure 5.13 is designed to allow water 
vapour to diffuse readily into the ventilated subfloor space. In this approach, higher indoor 
water vapour levels are intended to be dissipated through subfloor ventilation. 
However, experience in air-conditioned housing in the United States, has shown that this 
strategy can lead to moisture problems under summer conditions. In these cases, a 
reverse (inward) vapour drive can occur, where moist air from the subfloor migrates 
upward towards the cooler interior (Lstiburek 2008). 
As this moisture migrates upward, condensation may form on surfaces with high vapour 
resistance, such as vinyl flooring or the bases of furniture and cupboards in direct contact 
with the floor. Moisture accumulation within fibrous insulation can also result in elevated 
RH, increasing the risk of mould growth and timber decay in floor framing. 
One proposed mitigation strategy is the installation of foil-faced foam insulating board 
beneath the floor joists to act as a vapour control layer (see Figure 5.13). This approach 
relies on achieving a continuous airtight and vapour-tight installation which can be difficult 
to achieve in practice. 
If successfully sealed, the foil-faced insulation layer may also restrict downward drying. 
This restriction can increase the risk of trapping liquid moisture resulting from leaks or 
spills above the floor. These trade-offs highlight the importance of carefully assessing 
local climate conditions, building use and moisture sources before adopting vapour control 
measures under floors.

5.9 Risk assessment calculation methods and software 
Condensation risk within building assemblies can be assessed using a range of calculation 
methods and software tools. These methods are commonly grouped into steady-state and 
transient approaches. 
Both approaches are designed to model moisture behaviour within building elements. 
However, they differ significantly in their underlying assumptions, level of complexity, and 
the physical processes they are able to represent. As a result, they are suited to different 
types of assessment and design stages and levels of detail. 
The following sections outline the key characteristics of each approach and discuss their 
typical applications and limitations when assessing condensation risk. 
5.9.1 Steady -state methods 
Steady-state methods assess condensation risk by modelling the diffusion of water 
vapour through the materials and spaces of a building envelope. This is done by 
comparing the calculated dew point (or water vapour pressure) of the diffusing water 
vapour with the temperature of the surfaces it passes through. 
In these methods, water vapour is assumed to follow a simple, one-dimensional path 
through the assembly. As vapour diffuses through successive layers, its water vapour 
pressure decreases in proportion to the vapour resistance of each material layer. 
Steady-state methods assume indoor and outdoor air temperatures and dew points remain 
constant over the assessment period. In practice, this is typically represented using 
monthly average temperatures and dew points, with results accumulated over the course 
of a typical year. 
Steady-state condensation calculations can be performed manually and are often 
presented graphically, showing temperature and dew point (or partial water vapour 
pressure) profiles through the building assembly (see Figure 5.14).

5.9.2 Transient methods 
Transient condensation risk assessment methods aim to represent the dynamic interaction 
between climate and building materials over time. They seek to reflect the complex reality 
of how heat, liquid water and water vapour move through and are stored within building 
assemblies. 
Unlike steady-state methods – which consider heat conduction and vapour diffusion under 
fixed conditions – transient methods model a wider range of interacting processes over 
time, including: 
• wetting by liquid water 
• storage of heat and moisture within materials 
• temperature effects associated with evaporation and condensation 
• changes in material properties as temperature and humidity (among other factors) 
vary over time. 
Because of this complexity, transient methods rely on computer‑based simulations. These 
models may represent building assemblies in one or two dimensions, depending on the 
level of detail required and the nature of the assessment.

Transient modelling requires extensive input data, including detailed climate information 
and material properties. The reliability of results depends not only on the quality of this 
data, but also on the modeller’s understanding of building physics principles and the 
implications of modelling assumptions and input choices. Australian-specific climate 
databases should be used to ensure relevance. 
Both steady-state and transient methods have limitations. In particular, most modelling 
tools do not explicitly represent bulk air leakage paths or the water vapour transported 
with uncontrolled airflow. These effects are typically addressed through design 
assumptions rather than direct simulation. 
Within these limitations, transient tools continue to be developed and refined based on 
experience from research and practice. When applied appropriately by experienced 
practitioners, they can provide useful insights into: 
• the persistence of adverse combinations of indoor and outdoor conditions 
• the relative performance of alternative construction assemblies 
• the seasonal and long-term moisture behaviour of the building envelope.12 
 
Alert 
Transient condensation assessment methods and associated software require specialist 
expertise and careful interpretation. Meaningful results depend on informed modelling 
choices, appropriate input data and professional judgement. Accordingly, engagement of 
suitably qualified and experienced professionals is recommended.

6 Useful tips for design, construction and 
occupancy of buildings 
Effective management of condensation and moisture is essential to maintaining building 
durability, energy efficiency, and occupant wellbeing throughout a building’s life. 
This chapter provides practical guidance to help designers, builders, and occupants 
minimise condensation risks across the entire building lifecycle: 
• during design , through informed material selection, detailing and performance 
strategies 
• during construction , through appropriate installation, sequencing and quality control. 
 
Reminder 
Condensation risk is affected not only by design and construction, but also by how a 
building is occupied and used. Detailed consideration of occupancy and operational 
factors is outside the scope of this document. 
 
The guidance in this chapter is intended to complement earlier chapters by translating key 
principles into practical considerations. Unless otherwise stated, the information is 
explanatory and should be read alongside the relevant NCC provisions.

• Consider intended activities, occupancy patterns and likely sources of water vapour. 
Where future use is uncertain or may change, adopt conservative (worst-case) 
assumptions for moisture generation and operating conditions. 
Identify climate separation within the envelope 
• Determine where control layers establish the boundary between indoor and outdoor 
environments within the building envelope. Use this information to determine critical 
surface temperatures and undertake preliminary checks of interstitial condensation 
risk. 
6.1.2 Designing the building envelope 
Vapour resistance and drying potential 
• Confirm that the vapour resistance of control layers within proposed floor, wall, and 
roof assemblies complies with NCC requirements. Identify the layer with the highest 
vapour resistance and ensure that other layers have substantially lower resistances. 
Arrange layers to support drying to the inside, outside, or both as appropriate to the 
climate and assembly type. 
Surface temperature control 
• Design the assemblies so that critical surfaces – such as wall wraps, or sheathing 
located on the exterior side of insulated stud frames – remain above the indoor dew 
point under relevant design conditions. Account for the effect of insulation on both 
sides of these surfaces, including the thermal resistance of reflective surfaces facing 
still air spaces. 
Services and ventilation requirements 
• The following design considerations support NCC compliance and effective moisture 
and condensation management: 
• Consider providing adequate ventilation for water-heating systems installed within 
subfloor spaces. 
• Vent flue gases from boilers and water-heating systems directly to the exterior, 
including systems installed in non-habitable spaces, garages, subfloor spaces, and 
roof spaces. 
• Ensure mechanical exhaust air from bathrooms, laundries, and kitchens is discharged 
beyond the exterior wall or roof in accordance with the NCC.

6.1.3 Communicating the condensation control strategy 
Explain the design intent 
• Clearly communicate the condensation and moisture-control strategy to the builder 
and, where appropriate, support its implementation during construction. This should 
include the relevant strategies, materials, performance data and critical detailing 
needed to: 
• minimise the risk of internal surface condensation (including control of thermal 
bridging), and 
• limit the risk of interstitial condensation (including air-leakage control and correct 
installation of membranes or sheet materials that comply with specified limits for 
water vapour transmission resistance). 
Clarify membrane roles and limitations 
• Explain the purpose, required performance and limitations of all membranes and 
sheet materials installed between the internal lining and external cladding. Clearly 
identify which layers may be penetrated for services and which must remain 
continuous and unpenetrated to function as control layers. 
Verify installation 
• Where appropriate, confirm that control layers and materials are installed in 
accordance with the design intent and specifications. Ensure that any design or 
construction changes are reviewed to assess their potential impact on condensation 
risk. 
Document and hand over 
• Record the final condensation control strategy, including any approved changes 
made during construction, and clearly communicate the key features to building 
owners and occupants as part of handover documentation. 
Support occupant moisture management 
• Where appropriate, provide local source extraction and incorporate background or 
trickle ventilation to help occupants manage moisture levels during normal building

6.2 Construction tips 
6.2.1 Confirming the design intent before construction 
Identify what matters and why 
• Where not already provided, seek clear advice from the designer on which elements 
of the design are critical to managing condensation risk and why they are important. 
This helps ensure that critical elements are understood and prioritised during 
construction. 
Understand the intended control layers 
• Condensation strategies often rely on separate layers to manage liquid water, air, 
water vapour, and heat within the building envelope. Confirm the intended role and 
performance of each control layer and clarify any uncertainties with the designer 
before work begins. 
Confirm assembly requirements 
• Different condensation strategies may apply to roofs, walls, and floors, and may vary 
within the same element where construction details change. Confirm with the 
designer the exact location, continuity and specification of all relevant control layers 
and materials for each situation. 
Review existing buildings 
• Where alterations or additions are proposed, consider existing construction and 
moisture-management measures, including: 
• identifying any existing strategies used to minimise condensation risk that may be 
retained 
• where documentation is unavailable, consider assessing whether: 
• roof spaces were designed to be ventilated or airtight 
• penetrations through linings were sealed or unsealed 
• membranes or sheet materials were used to control air or water vapour movement in 
walls, roofs, or floors.

6.2.2 Maintaining the design intent during construction 
Communicate with all relevant trades 
• Brief site personnel responsible for installing critical materials on the condensation 
control strategy. Ensure all trades – particularly services installers – understand which 
layers must not be penetrated, altered or substituted. 
Manage construction moisture 
• Sequence wet trades (such as slabs, screeds, plastering, jointing, tiling) to allow 
maximum drying time before enclosure or application of finishes. 
Avoid unapproved material changes 
• Do not substitute, remove, or add materials that affect condensation control without 
designer approval. Seemingly beneficial changes, such as extra insulation or 
waterproofing, can increase condensation risk if they restrict drying or alter dew 
point conditions. Ensure the specified performance requirements for critical materials 
are clearly documented and understood. 
Respond to unexpected site conditions 
• Notify the designer if unexpected groundwater or wet ground conditions are 
encountered during excavation. Seek direction on managing moisture and preventing 
water accumulation beneath or against the building. 
Protect materials on site 
• Keep materials dry before installation by protecting them from: 
• rain and surface water runoff 
• damp rising from the ground 
• condensation dripping from sheltering roofs or temporary coverings (such as 
tarpaulins) placed over materials stored on uncovered ground. 
Avoid enclosure of wet materials 
• Do not install wet materials. Protect installed materials from rain, dew, and wet site 
activities. If materials become wet, allow them to dry fully before enclosure, 
especially for materials that absorb water such as insulation, plasterboard, masonry, 
timber and wood-based products.

Maintain ventilation pathways 
• Confirm that all ventilation pathways specified in the design remain unobstructed 
during construction and are clear at handover. Check that ventilation openings and 
weepholes remain clear especially during installation of insulation. 
Provide ventilation during construction 
• Where safe and appropriate, keep trickle ventilators and other secure openings open 
until handover, particularly when the building is sealed overnight. If internal surface 
condensation is observed, consider additional temporary ventilation or 
dehumidification. 
6.2.3 Communicating the condensation control strategy at handover 
Explain the drying out period 
• Inform building users that moisture introduced during construction may take a year or 
more to dissipate fully. Explain that appropriate ventilation is particularly important 
during early occupation to assist drying and reduce the risk of condensation. 
Explain installed ventilation features 
• Identify and explain the purpose and correct use of: 
• bathroom, laundry, and kitchen exhaust systems 
• any ventilation provided beyond NCC minimum requirements (for example, trickle 
ventilators incorporated in window systems). 
• Emphasise how these features help manage indoor moisture during normal 
occupation. 
Highlight external ventilation openings 
• Identify ventilation openings serving subfloor spaces, wall cavities and roof spaces. 
Explain the need to keep these openings clear and unobstructed, including avoiding 
blockage by landscaping, garden beds, stored items, plants or creepers, as 
obstruction can increase condensation and moisture-related risks.

Appendix C Compliance with the NCC 
C.1 Responsibilities for regulation of building and 
plumbing in Australia 
State and territory governments are responsible for regulation of building, plumbing and 
development/planning in their respective state or territory. 
The NCC is a joint initiative of the Commonwealth and State and Territory Governments in 
Australia and is produced and maintained by the ABCB on behalf of the Australian 
Government and each state and territory government. The NCC provides a uniform set of 
technical provisions for the design and construction of buildings and other structures, and 
plumbing and drainage systems throughout Australia. It allows for variations in climate and 
geological or geographic conditions. 
The NCC is given legal effect by building and plumbing regulatory legislation in each state 
and territory. This legislation consists of an Act of Parliament and subordinate legislation 
(e.g. building regulations) which empowers the regulation of certain aspects of buildings 
and structures, and contains the administrative provisions necessary to give effect to the 
legislation. 
Each state and territory's legislation adopts the NCC subject to the variation or deletion of 
some of its provisions, or the addition of extra provisions. These variations, deletions and 
additions are generally signposted within the relevant section of the NCC, and located 
within appendices to the NCC. Notwithstanding this, any provision of the NCC may be 
overridden by, or subject to, state or territory legislation. The NCC must therefore be read 
in conjunction with that legislation. 
C.2 Demonstrating compliance with the NCC 
Compliance with the NCC is achieved by complying with the NCC Governing 
Requirements and relevant Performance Requirements. 
The Governing Requirements are a set of governing rules outlining how the NCC must be 
used and the process that must be followed. 
The Performance Requirements prescribe the minimum necessary requirements for 
buildings, building elements, and plumbing and drainage systems. They must be met to 
demonstrate compliance with the NCC.

Appendix D Standards 
This appendix covers key Australian and international standards relevant to condensation. 
There is no Australian Standard that solely addresses the management of condensation. 
However, standards dealing with roofing, wall cladding, insulation, masonry, and bushfire 
management, all influence how designers and builders manage condensation-related 
issues. 
There are international standards that specifically address condensation. These standards 
are generally developed for European climate conditions and are often based on 
construction practices that are not common in Australia. As a result, designers should 
carefully consider their applicability before relying on international Standards in an 
Australian context. 
 
Alert 
The standards referenced in this section may be updated from time to time. For NCC 
referenced standards, users should refer to the NCC list of referenced documents to 
identify the applicable version. For other standards, the latest edition in force at the time 
of application should be confirmed independently.

About NCC Volume One 
NCC Volume One contains technical design and construction requirements for all Class 2 to 9 buildings (multi-residential, 
commercial, industrial, and public assembly buildings) and their associated structures. 
NCC Volume One contains the requirements for— 
all Class 2 to 9 buildings; and •
access requirements for people with a disability in Class 1b and 10a buildings; and •
certain Class 10b structures including access requirements for people with a disability in Class 10b swimming pools. •
Components of NCC Volume One 
NCC Volume One contains the following Sections: 
Section A – Governing Requirements •
Section B – Structure •
Section C – Fire resistance •
Section D – Access and egress •
Section E – Services and equipment •
Section F – Health and amenity •
Section G – Ancillary provisions •
Section I – Special use buildings •
Section J – Energy efficiency •
Schedules— •
Abbreviations and symbols ◾
Definitions ◾
Referenced documents ◾
State and Territory variations and additions ◾
Section A contains the mandatory Governing Requirements for the NCC. Sections B to G and I to J contain the mandatory 
Performance Requirements and the pathways that can be used to comply with the NCC. 
There is no Section H in NCC Volume One because the letter ‘H’ is used in NCC Volume Two. This avoids number clashes 
between NCC Volume One and NCC Volume Two.

Introduction to this Part 
This Part explains the evidence needed to show that the NCC requirements are met and the solution is “fit for purpose”. 
It covers the use of materials, products, forms of construction and designs. It details separate requirements for the BCA 
and PCA. 
Examples of evidence to be prepared and retained include certificates, reports, calculations and any other documents or 
information showing compliance with the NCC requirements. 
 
 
 
 A5G1 Suitability 
 
(1) A building and plumbing or drainage installation must be constructed using materials, products, plumbing products, 
forms of construction and designs fit for their intended purpose to achieve the relevant requirements of the NCC. 
(2) For the purposes of (1), a material, product, plumbing product, form of construction or design is fit for purpose if it 
is— 
supported by evidence of suitability in accordance with— (a)
A5G2; and (i)
A5G3 or A5G4 as appropriate; and (ii)
constructed or installed in an appropriate manner. (b)
 
Explanatory Information 
A5G1 relates to the quality of work and materials needed to construct a building to meet NCC requirements. 
This means that— 
all people involved with construction must work skillfully in accordance with good trade practice; and •
all materials must be of a quality to fulfil their function/s within the building. •
A5G1 only applies to matters normally covered by the NCC. 
While A5G1 outlines quality of work and material demands, sometimes additional conditions may be required by— 
other Commonwealth, State or Territory legislation; and •
contracts that include either specific quality requirements, or requirements for specific materials and the like. •
 
Explanatory Information: Example 
Permit authorities would ordinarily not apply A5G1 to such matters as— 
plastering — other than for fire rating, waterproofing of wet areas, and sound insulation; or •
painting — other than that required for weatherproofing an external wall. •
When determining which form of evidence will be used, it is important to consider the appropriateness of the evidence, 
as some forms of evidence may be more suitable to materials and products and others to designs and forms of 
construction. The requirement to consider appropriateness of the evidence is specified in A5G2(1).

Introduction to this Part 
The NCC groups buildings and structures by the purpose for which they are designed, constructed or adapted to be used, 
assigning each type of building or structure with a classification. This Part explains how each building classification is 
defined and used in the NCC. 
The building classifications are labelled “Class 1” through to “Class 10”. Some classifications also have sub-classifications, 
referred to by a letter after the number (e.g. Class 1a). 
The technical building requirements for Class 2 to 9 buildings are mostly covered by Volume One of the NCC and those 
for Class 1 and 10 are mostly covered by Volume Two of the NCC. Volume Three of the NCC covers plumbing and drainage 
requirements for all building classifications. 
A building may have parts that have been designed, constructed or adapted for different purposes. In most cases, each 
of these parts is a separate classification. A building (or part of a building) may also have more than one such purpose 
and may be assigned more than one classification. 
 
 
 
 A6G1 Determining a building classification 
 
(1) The classification of a building or part of a building is determined by the purpose for which it is designed, constructed 
or adapted to be used. 
(2) Each part of a building must be classified according to its purpose and comply with all the appropriate requirements 
for its classification. 
(3) A room that contains a mechanical, thermal or electrical facility or the like that serves the building must have the 
same classification as the major part or principal use of the building or fire compartment in which it is situated. 
(4) Unless another classification is more suitable, an occupiable outdoor area must have the same classification as the 
part of the building to which it is associated. 
 
Exemptions 
For A6G1(1) where a part of a building has been designed, constructed or adapted for a different purpose and is (1)
less than 10% of the floor area of the storey it is situated on, the classification of the other part of the storey may 
apply to the whole storey. 
A6G1(3) does not apply to an electricity network substation. (2)
 
Limitations 
Exemption (1) does not apply where the minor use of a building is a laboratory, a Class 9b early childhood centre, or a 
Class 2, 3 or 4 part of a building. 
 
Explanatory Information 
Classification is a process for understanding risks in a building or part, according to its use. It must be correctly 
undertaken to achieve NCC aims as appropriate to each building in each circumstance. 
It is possible for a single building to have parts with different classifications. Part of a building can also have more than 
one classification. Where there is any conflict between what requirements the part should comply with, the more stringent 
requirement applies. 
Where it is unclear which classification should apply, appropriate authorities have the discretion to decide. They base 
their decision on an assessment of the building proposal.

They will look at what classification the building most closely resembles. They will also take into account the likely fire 
load, plus, the likely consequences of any risks to the safety, health and amenity of people using the building. 
Appropriate authorities will also look at any relevant court decisions or determinations of the State or Territory body 
responsible for considering appeals on building classification matters. 
It should be noted that appeals body determinations and, in some States and Territories, certain court decisions are 
usually not precedent creating. Such decisions are determined on a case-by-case basis. 
It should also be noted that State and Territory authorities responsible for building regulatory matters may have issued 
advice, interpretations or guidelines to assist practitioners in applying the correct classification to a building or part. 
Advice on such matters should be sought from the relevant authority. 
Under Exemption (1) to A6G1, if 10% or less of the floor area of a storey is used for a purpose which could be classified 
differently to the remainder of that storey, that part may be classified as being the same as the remainder. Laboratories, 
sole-occupancy units in Class 2, 3 or 4 parts, and Class 9b early childhood centres are excluded from this concession 
(see Limitation to A6G1). The reason is that laboratories are considered to have a high fire hazard potential and 
classifying them with the remainder of the building could, in a majority of cases, endanger occupants of the other parts 
of the building which have a lower fire hazard potential. In relation to Class 9b early childhood centres, the intent is to 
ensure that these facilities cannot be regarded as another class and that the specific fire safety requirements applicable 
to Class 9b early childhood centres are implemented. Also, the intent is not to allow sole-occupancy units in Class 2, 3 
or 4 parts to be regarded as another Class such as Class 6 and then not have any fire or sound insulation between the 
units and any other classification which may have a high fire load and could endanger the occupants of the Class 2, 3 
or 4 part. 
If Exemption (1) to A6G1 is used, it should be remembered that it will still be necessary to use the occupant numbers 
in Volume One Table D2D18 for the particular use of the area. Likewise, the lighting and equipment levels, people 
occupancy and load profiles for the area of minor use for the purposes of Volume One Section J must be in accordance 
with the use of the area. 
If the storey has a very large floor area, the 10% or less concession area may also be large, even though the rest of 
the building is classifiable as a building which ordinarily has a lower risk potential. An example of the application of this 
area concession could be as follows: 
If a single storey factory has an office that takes up 8% of the whole storey’s floor area, the entire building (including •
the office) can be classified as being Class 8. 
However, if that office area takes up 12% of the storey’s floor area, that area must be classified as Class 5, and the •
remainder of the building as Class 8. 
Under A6G1(3) a plant room, machinery room, lift motor room or boiler room, have the same classification as the part 
of the building they are in. These kinds of rooms do not need to be ancillary or subordinate to the part of the building 
they are in, that is, the 10% criterion is not applicable. 
There are specific provisions for these kinds of rooms. For example, Volume One Section C requires some of them to 
be fire separated from the remainder of the building (e.g. see C3D14 with regard to elements of the electricity supply 
system).

 S9C1 Scope 
 
This Specification sets out requirements for cavity barriers in fire-protected timber construction. 
 S9C2 Requirements 
 
(1) Cavity barriers must be provided in the following locations where fire-protected timber is used in any of the listed 
elements: 
At concealed cavities adjacent to junctions between fire-resisting floor/ceiling assemblies and fire-resisting walls. (a)
At concealed cavities adjacent to junctions between fire-resisting floor/ceiling assemblies and fire-resisting or (b)
non-combustible external walls. 
At concealed cavities adjacent to junctions between fire-resisting walls and fire-resisting or non-combustible (c)
external walls. 
Around the perimeter of door and window openings in fire-resisting construction. (d)
(2) Cavity barriers must be installed so they are tight fitting and are able to withstand thermal expansion and structural 
movement without the loss of seal against fire and smoke. 
(3) In addition to cavity barriers required by (1), horizontal and vertical cavity barriers are to be provided to wall cavities 
within, around or adjacent to fire-protected timber elements as follows: 
Horizontal cavity barriers — at not more than 5 m centres. (a)
Vertical cavity barriers — at not more than 10 m centres. (b)
(4) Cavity barriers must— 
achieve the performance specified in Table S9C2 based on the highest FRL of the elements they are mounted (a)
within or seal against; or 
consist of— (b)
timber with the minimum thickness specified in Table S9C2; or (i)
polythene-sleeved mineral wool or mineral wool slabs or strips placed under compression to achieve the (ii)
minimum thickness specified in Table S9C2. 
(5) Cavity barriers provided around openings may be formed by the window or door frame if— 
the frame is constructed of steel or timber with the minimum thickness specified in Table S9C2 for timber; and (a)
the frame is tightly fitted to rigid construction and mechanically fixed in position. (b)
(6) The FRL of cavity barriers in fire-protected timber construction must be determined in accordance with Specifications 
1 and 2 applying the criteria for control joint systems specified in Section 10 of AS 1530.4 with the cavity barrier 
system fitted within an opening between timber members exposed directly to the furnace heating conditions. 
(7) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in Specifications 1 and 2 or AS 1530.4, the test results from (6) may be used 
when the fire-protected timber is constructed from timber having a nominal density at least equal to the tested timber.

This Specification contains requirements for fire-protected timber and procedures for determining the time at which the 
temperature at the interface between the protection system and the timber is exceeded. 
 
 
 
 S10C2 General requirements

which consists of not less than 2 layers of 13 mm thick, fire-protective grade plasterboard. (ii)

 S10C3 Massive timber

not less than that specified by Table S10C3; and (ii)
has any cavity filled with non-combustible insulation, or no cavity, between— (c)

timber elements within the fire-protective covering. (ii)

 S13C1 Scope 
 
This Specification prescribes materials and methods of installation for services that penetrate walls, floors and ceilings 
required to have an FRL. 
 S13C2 Application 
 
(1) This Specification applies to installations permitted under the Deemed-to-Satisfy Provisions of the NCC as alternatives 
to systems that have been demonstrated by test to fulfil the requirements of C4D15(2)(a). 
(2) This Specification does not apply to installations in ceilings required to have a resistance to the incipient spread of 
fire nor to the installation of piping that contains or is intended to contain a flammable liquid or gas. 
 S13C3 Metal pipe systems 
 
(1) A pipe system comprised entirely of metal (excluding pipe seals or the like) that is not normally filled with liquid must 
not be located within 100 mm, for a distance of 2 m from the penetration, of any combustible building element or a 
position where combustible material may be located, and must be constructed of— 
copper alloy or stainless steel with a wall thickness of at least 1 mm; or (a)
cast iron or steel (other than stainless steel) with a wall thickness of at least 2 mm. (b)
(2) An opening for a pipe system comprised entirely of metal (excluding pipe seals or the like) must— 
be neatly formed, cut or drilled; and (a)
be no closer than 200 mm to any other service penetration; and (b)
accommodate only one pipe. (c)
(3) A pipe system comprised entirely of metal (excluding pipe seals or the like) must be wrapped but must not be lagged 
or enclosed in thermal insulation over the length of its penetration of a wall, floor or ceiling unless the lagging or 
thermal insulation fulfils the requirements of S13C7. 
(4) The gap between a metal pipe and the wall, floor or ceiling it penetrates must be fire-stopped in accordance with 
S13C7. 
 S13C4 Pipes penetrating sanitary compartments 
 
If a pipe of metal or UPVC penetrates the floor of a sanitary compartment in accordance with C4D15(2)(c)(ii)— 
the opening must be neatly formed and no larger than is necessary to accommodate the pipe or fitting; and (a)
the gap between pipe and floor must be fire-stopped in accordance with S13C7. (b)
 S13C5 Wires and cables 
 
If a wire or cable or cluster of wires or cables penetrates a floor, wall or ceiling— 
the opening must be neatly formed, cut or drilled and no closer than 50 mm to any other service; and (a)

Introduction to this Part 
This Part is intended to reduce the likelihood of illness or loss of amenity as result of undue noise transmission between 
different parts of a building or adjoining buildings. This Part contains minimum requirements for sound insulation for walls, 
floors and penetrations through walls and floors for services such as pipework. 
 
 
 
 F7O1 Objective 
 
The Objective of this Part is to safeguard occupants from illness or loss of amenity as a result of undue sound being 
transmitted— 
between adjoining sole-occupancy units; and (a)
from common spaces to sole-occupancy units; and (b)
from parts of different classifications to sole-occupancy units. (c)
 
Applications 
F7O1 only applies to a Class 2 or 3 building or a Class 9c building.

a sole-occupancy unit from a common space, (c)

to allow outward drying of internal moisture. In tropical climates, materials with a relatively lower vapour permeance

Open-cell insulation, such as mineral wool or fibreglass, typically has a high vapour permeance , while closed-cell 
insulation such as polystyrene typically has a low vapour permeance.

that form part of the building envelope of sole-occupancy units in climate zones 6, 7 and 8 to incorporate a drained and 
vented cavity, unless the wall is constructed from insulated sandwich panels. 
Devices which restrict vermin entry or service penetrations may be used if they facilitate drainage and ventilation as 
required by this Part.

Ventilation openings are specified as a minimum free open area per metre length. The longest total plan dimension (1)
is based on the roof length irrespective of the number of storeys beneath. 
Total low level ventilation openings are calculated based on twice the longest total plan dimension of the roof, (2)
except for mono pitch or skillion roofs that are calculated based on the longest total plan dimension of the roof. 
Total high level ventilation is calculated based on the longest total plan dimension of the roof. 
High level openings are openings provided at the ridge or not more than 900 mm below the ridge or highest point (3)
of the roof space, measured vertically or 1/3 of the height of the roof below highest point of the roof, whichever is 
least. 
 
Explanatory Information 
Ventilation openings are to be evenly distributed to avoid creating pockets of stagnant air. 
Multi-storey construction does not require the duplication of the longest plan dimension of a roof for the purposes of 
calculating the ventilation opening requirement. 
Openings created by roof cladding profile can help meet ventilation opening requirements. Examples include openings 
underneath a metal cladding profile or inherent openings in a profiled tile roof, provided these openings are directly 
connected to the roof void to be ventilated and remain unobstructed. 
Typical fasteners used in roofing application that may intrude into the ventilation open area will not cause excessive 
resistance to airflow. Components such as spacers, battens and the like greater than 18 mm in height are acceptable 
provided they do not create excessive resistance to airflow. Components such as meshes which may restrict the entry 
of vermin, ember or corrosive aerosols, or the like may also be used if they facilitate drainage and ventilation as required 
by this part. 
For roof pitches greater than 10 degrees, total low level ventilation openings must be greater than total high level 
ventilation openings to minimise drawing air from occupied spaces and ensure intake of outdoor air. For roof pitches 
less than 10 degrees (excluding skillion roofs), ventilation of the roof space is facilitated by cross ventilation at opposing 
ends. High level ventilation is not necessary.

Introduction to this Part 
This Part sets the thermal performance properties of building fabric, the energy efficiency of key energy using equipment 
and the features a building must have to facilitate the future installation of distributed energy resources. 
 
Notes 
For Class 2 buildings, Section J is replaced with Section J of NCC 2022 Amendment 2. 
 
Notes 
In Tasmania, for a Class 2 building and Class 4 part of a building, Section J is replaced with Section J of BCA 2019 
Amendment 1. For all other classes Section J is replaced with Section J of BCA 2022 Amendment 2. 
 
 
 
 J1O1 Objective 
 
The Objective of this Section is to— 
reduce energy consumption and energy peak demand; and (a)
reduce greenhouse gas emissions; and (b)
improve occupant health and amenity. (c)
 
 
 
 J1F1 Energy efficiency 
 
A building must— 
reduce the energy consumption and energy peak demand of key energy using equipment; and (a)
reduce the greenhouse gas emissions that occur as a result of a building’s energy consumption and energy (b)
source; and 
for a Class 4 part of a building, improve occupant health and amenity by mitigating the impact of extreme hot (c)
and cold weather events and energy blackouts; and 
for other than in a Class 4 part of a building, protect occupant health and amenity by ensuring the building (d)
envelope assists in the maintenance of acceptable internal conditions while the building is occupied; and 
be able to accommodate the installation of distributed energy resources. (e)

 J1P1 Operational energy use and greenhouse gas emissions 
 
A building, other than a Class 4 part of a building, including its services, must have features that— 
facilitate the efficient use of energy and near zero operational greenhouse gas emissions appropriate to— (a)
the function and use of the building; and (i)
the level of human comfort required for the building use; and (ii)
for the conditioned space, achieve an hourly regulated energy consumption and associated greenhouse gas (b)
emission, averaged over the annual hours of operation, of not more than— 
for a Class 6 building, 40 kJ/m².hr and 4 g of CO2-e/m2.hr; and (i)
for a Class 5, 7b, 8 or 9a building other than a ward area, or a Class 9b school, 22 kJ/m².hr and 2.2 g of (ii)
CO2-e/m2.hr; and 
for all other building classifications, 8 kJ/m².hr and 1 g of CO2-e/m2.hr. (iii)
 J1P2 Thermal performance of a Class 4 part of a building 
 
(1) The total heating load of the habitable rooms and conditioned spaces in a Class 4 part of a building must not exceed 
the heating load limit in Specification 44. 
(2) The total cooling load of the habitable rooms and conditioned spaces in a Class 4 part of a building must not exceed 
the cooling load limit in Specification 44. 
(3) The total thermal energy load of the habitable rooms and conditioned spaces in a Class 4 part of a building must not 
exceed the thermal energy load limit in Specification 44. 
 J1P3 Energy usage of a Class 4 part of a building 
 
(1) The energy value of the domestic services of a Class 4 part of a building must not exceed the energy value with— 
a 3-star ducted heat pump, rated under the 2019 GEMS determination, heating all spaces that are provided with (a)
heating; and 
a 3-star ducted heat pump, rated under the 2019 GEMS determination, cooling all spaces that are provided with (b)
cooling; and 
a 5-star instantaneous gas water heater, rated under the 2017 GEMS determination, providing all domestic hot (c)
water; and 
a lighting power density of 4 W/m2 serving all internal spaces that are provided with artificial lighting. (d)
(2) Domestic services, including any associated distribution system and components must, to the degree necessary, 
have features that facilitate the efficient use of energy appropriate to— 
the domestic service and its usage; and (a)
the geographic location of the building; and (b)
the location of the domestic service; and (c)
the energy source. (d)
 J1P4 Renewable energy, energy storage and electric vehicle charging 
 
A building must have features that facilitate the future installation of on-site renewable energy generation and energy 
storage equipment, except where this is already installed to the maximum practicable extent, and electric vehicle charging 
equipment.

 S36C1 Scope 
 
This Specification lists the thermal properties of some common construction materials. 
 S36C2 Construction Deemed-to-Satisfy 
 
(1) Tables S36C2a, S36C2b, S36C2c, S36C2d and S36C2e list the thermal conductivity considered to be achieved by 
some common construction materials. 
(2) For the purposes of Tables S36C2a, S36C2b, S36C2c, S36C2d and S36C2e: 
For materials which incorporate cores or hollows in regular patterns (such as cored brickwork, hollow blockwork (a)
and cored floor or wall panels), the tabulated material densities and thermal conductivities are based on the 
gross density (mass divided by external dimensions). 
The R-Value of a material is determined by dividing the thickness of the material in metres by the thermal (b)
conductivity in Wm-1K-1. 
(3) Tables S36C2f, S36C2g, S36C2h, S36C2i, S36C2j, S36C2k, S36C2l and S36C2m list the R-Value considered to be 
achieved by air films and airspaces. 
(4) For an envelope that contains a ventilated airspace, the Total R-Value of the building fabric must be reduced based 
on the area of ventilation openings in accordance with clause 6.3 of AS/NZS 4859.2. 
(5) The requirements of (4) do not apply to a roof with an airspace greater than 300 mm or a pitched roof greater than 
5° with a horizontal ceiling.

 S37C1 Scope 
 
This specification describes the methods of calculating the U-Value and solar admittance of a wall-glazing construction. 
 S37C2 General 
 
For determining the aspect of a wall-glazing construction— 
the northern aspect is within 45° of true north; and (a)
the southern aspect is within 45° of true south; and (b)
the eastern aspect is within 45° of true east; and (c)
the western aspect is within 45° of true west. (d)
 S37C3 U-Value — Method 1 (Single Aspect) 
 
(1) For the purposes of this method, a wall-glazing construction only includes the walls and glazing facing a single aspect. 
(2) The Total System U-Value of the wall component of a wall-glazing construction must be calculated as the inverse of 
the Total R-Value, including allowance for thermal bridging, in accordance with— 
AS/NZS 4859.2; or (a)
Specification 38 for spandrel panels. (b)
(3) The Total System U-Value of a wall-glazing construction must be calculated as the area-weighted average of the 
Total System U-Value of each of the components of the wall-glazing construction. 
 S37C4 U-Value — Method 2 (Multiple Aspects) 
 
(1) For the purposes of this method, a wall-glazing construction only includes the walls and glazing facing multiple 
aspects. 
(2) The Total System U-Value of the wall component of a wall-glazing construction must be calculated as the inverse of 
the Total R-Value, including allowance for thermal bridging, in accordance with— 
AS/NZS 4859.2; or (a)
Specification 38 for spandrel panels. (b)
(3) The Total System U-Value of a wall-glazing construction must be calculated as the area-weighted average of the 
Total System U-Value of each of the components of the wall-glazing construction.

 S40C1 Scope 
 
This Specification contains the requirements for lighting and power control devices including manual switches, time 
switches, demand-operated controls and daylight control devices. 
 S40C2 Manual switch 
 
An artificial lighting manual switch must be located in a visible and easily accessed position— 
in the room or space being switched; or (a)
in an adjacent room or space from where at least 90% of the lighting being controlled is visible. (b)
 
 S40C3 Time switch 
 
(1) A time switch must— 
be capable of switching on and off electric power at variable pre-programmed times and on variable pre-(a)
programmed days; and 
have the ability to program public holidays at least 1 year ahead. (b)
(2) A time switch for internal lighting must be capable of being overridden by— 
a demand-operated control; or (a)
a manual switch. (b)
(3) A time switch for external lighting must be capable of being configured to limit the period the system is switched on 
to between 30 minutes before sunset and 30 minutes after sunrise. 
(4) A time switch for boiling water or chilled water storage units must be capable of being overridden for a maximum 
period of 2 hours outside normal operating hours. 
 S40C4 Demand-operated control 
 
(1) A demand-operated control must— 
activate artificial lighting upon detecting the presence or movement of an occupant; and (a)
deactivate artificial lighting immediately or after a run-on period not more than 15 minutes after the space is (b)
vacated. 
(2) A demand-operated control in a fire-isolated stairway , fire-isolated passageway or fire-isolated ramp must be 
configured so that a minimum of 30% of the full design illumination is provided when deactivation required by (1)(b) 
has occurred. 
 
Notes 
For the purposes of S40C4, demand-operated controls may detect the presence or movement of an occupant via a 
motion detector, key card, security system or the like.

 S48C1 Scope 
 
This Specification contains the requirements for comparing sensible heating and cooling loads for each assessable zone 
in the proposed building with the corresponding zones in the reference building. 
 S48C2 Comparison of zone loads in proposed building and reference building 
 
(1) The zone load is the sensible heating or cooling effect required to maintain the temperature in each zone within the 
range specified in S34C3(8). 
(2) The loads for each zone in the proposed building and the reference building must be calculated in accordance with 
the modelling parameters of Specification 34. 
(3) A zone of the proposed building is assessable under J1V3(1)(b)(iii) to (v) if it has— 
a 98th percentile heating load of at least 10 W/m2: or (a)
a 98th percentile cooling load of at least 40 W/m2.(b)

 Part B1 Structural provisions 
Delete B1P1 and insert NSW B1P1 as follows: 
 NSW B1P1 Structural reliability 
 
(1) By resisting the actions to which it may reasonably be expected to be subjected, a building or structure, during 
construction and use, with appropriate levels of reliability, must— 
perform adequately under all reasonably expected design actions; and (a)
withstand extreme or frequently repeated design actions; and (b)
be designed to sustain local damage, with the structural system as a whole remaining stable and not being (c)
damaged to an extent disproportionate to the original local damage; and 
avoid causing damage to other properties. (d)
(2) The actions to be considered to satisfy (1) and (2) include but are not limited to— 
permanent actions (dead loads) including, for a Class 7b building, an additional notional permanent roof load of (a)
not less than 0.15 kPa to support the addition of solar photovoltaic panels; and 
imposed actions (live loads arising from occupancy and use); and (b)
wind action; and (c)
earthquake action; and (d)
snow action; and (e)
liquid pressure action; and (f)
ground water action; and (g)
rainwater action (including ponding action); and (h)
earth pressure action; and (i)
differential movement; and (j)
time dependent effects (including creep and shrinkage); and (k)
thermal effects; and (l)
ground movement caused by— (m)
swelling, shrinkage or freezing of the subsoil; and (i)
landslip or subsidence; and (ii)
siteworks associated with the building or structure; and (iii)
construction activity actions; and (n)
termite actions. (o)

with a roof area of not more than 55 m2; or (b)
where more than 50% of the roof area is used as a terrace, carpark, roof garden, roof light or the like. (c)

Introduction to this Part 
This NSW Part J1 replaces Part J1. 
This Part sets the thermal performance properties of building fabric, the energy efficiency of key energy using equipment 
and the features a building must have to facilitate the future installation of distributed energy resources. 
 
Notes 
For a Class 2 building or a Class 4 part of a building, where a relevant development consent or an application for (1)
a complying development certificate requires compliance with a BASIX Single Dwelling or Multi Dwelling Certificate 
issued under Version 3.0 or earlier, NSW Section J of NCC 2019 Volume One Amendment 1 applies. 
For a Class 2 building or a Class 4 part of a building, where a relevant development consent or an application for (2)
a complying development certificate requires compliance with a BASIX Single Dwelling or Multi Dwelling Certificate 
issued under Version 4.0 or later, Section J of NCC 2022 Amendment 2 Volume One applies. 
For a Class 2 building or a Class 4 part of a building, where a relevant development consent or an application for (3)
a complying development certificate requires compliance with a BASIX Alterations and Additions Certificate, NSW 
Section J of NCC 2019 Volume One Amendment 1 applies. 
 
Notes 
In NSW, Class 2 buildings and Class 4 parts of buildings are subject to BASIX (the Building Sustainability Index), 
however Class 3 buildings are not. 
BASIX is the web-based planning tool designed to assess the potential performance of certain residential buildings 
against a range of sustainability indices including thermal comfort and energy. Commitments made under BASIX become 
a condition of the relevant development consent or complying development certificate. 
BASIX applies in NSW to all new Class 2 buildings and Class 4 parts of buildings; and to alterations and additions to 
buildings of those classes where the work is subject to BASIX and also where an applicant elects to comply with BASIX. 
The provisions of Section J are therefore designed to complement requirements that arise under BASIX and which are 
implemented via the development consent. 
Where BASIX is not applied to alterations and additions to these buildings, the provisions will also complement council 
development controls that require energy efficiency measures to be incorporated as part of the alterations and additions.

The Objective of this Section is to— 
reduce energy consumption and energy peak demand; and (a)
reduce greenhouse gas emissions; and (b)
improve occupant health and amenity. (c)
